Editor's Notes
Thanks go out to Bill Fowle for his information talk on transferring images to wood. If you
missed some of the details you can review to article in this issue. There are the regular FoF
and Tech Talk columns and Closer Look this month talked to Jay and Lin Mapson about
their recent collaboration pieces. Be sure to check out the details of Don Hoskins estate

We had a fun Tech Talk last month starting with Marteen showing off his “mini” lathes. He took the motor
from the zoom lens of a digital camera and built housing for it. He then attached a wire connector and balanced it to reduce vibrations. Material is connected to
the lathe with a set screw and files are used to shape the
wood. Marteen’s mini-world continues to amaze us.
Art R. reported that BC Auction ( https://
www.bcauction.ca ) has some very interesting items on
sale. This time it was several Delta dust collector units.
It is worth checking them out periodically as they sell of
government surplus equipment.
Brian asked where he could get a good vacuum gauge. I
had great success with John Sherman Agencies Ltd.,
1641 Venables Street Vancouver, BC V5L 2H1, Phone:
877-251-9622 or: 604-254-9622.
Pat D. brought in his Trent Bosch hollowing system to
show off. He reported that other suppliers were not
interested in giving him the advice he needed but that
Trent spend a long time on the phone helping him
through his purchase. Pat bought the smaller ½” system and is very happy with it. Check out Trent Bosch’s
website for more details - http://www.trentbosch.com/
catalog/
Robert reported good success in stabilizing some punky
wood with Minwax Wood Hardener from Rona. In
some stores this is an order online – deliver to the store
item while some stores stock it. He reports that it
seems to work well and has little effect on sanding and
finishing.
Tom B. reported a great hack for his Triton respirator.
The hose broke so he salvaged the connectors from
each end and used a piece of vacuum cleaner hose to
replace the broken part. Great idea, Tom!
Finally, we had a wide-ranging discussion on dust collection. The highlights include:

First priority is to collect the dust at source

Second is to wear a good mask/respirator

Third is to filter the ambient air with a personal
dust protection device .
It is important to size the unit to your needs and to ensure the unit is capable of filtering the amount of air the
system is drawing. If the filter system in inadequate
the most dangerous dust will simply be blown through
it back into your shop. The newer baffle canisters are a
better choice than cloth bags.
Managing the material that is collected is important
too. Where possible a cyclonic separator is worth the
additional cost. Also, many turners report that they do
not run their system to collect chips while turning but
wait to the sanding phase. Another hint is to clean out
the system regularly to keep it working at peak efficiency.
We often choose the forego dust management equipment in favour of turning tools. While this is natural
enough, it is really important to be as careful with our
lungs as we do with our eyes. COPD is a terrible way to
go.
Plan to join us for Tech Talk next month and bring
along your question, tricks, and tips.
Bruce Campbell

Focus On Fundamentals
Jamb Chucking a Bowl with Ed Pretty
Finishing off the bottom of a bowl is a challenge but
with a simple jam setup it can be quite straight forward.
Ed Pretty agreed to show us how in the Focus On Fundamentals session last month.
Ed started off by making a small bowl then mounted a
scrap of wood and faced it off flat. Then he measured
the bowl and used dividers to mark the face for a reference mark and high lighted with a pencil. This jamb
chuck will be used for removing the tendon and finishing the bottom of the bowl.
He then proceeded to explain about the pros and cons
of having a compression (external) fit or an expansion
(internal) fit. Expansion fit may crack the wood but it
will work.
He then started to turn stating that you should have a
flat at the bottom and a slight taper on the sides for
gripping the bowl.
The tip was to sneak up to the size needed. This will
align the bowl and drive the bowl with friction. If you
go too far you can use a water spray (temporary fix) or a
sheet or two of paper towel to grip the bowl.
He also mentioned that if you have trouble getting the
bowl you can tap the chuck or turn away the scrap
wood to loosen the bowl.
Ed uses his vacuum chuck as a jamb chuck often.
Jamb chucks are cheap and reusable with planning.
Thank you Ed.
Just a couple of links for Jamb Chucking.
http://kurthertzog.com/articles/
wt_245_34_36_workholdingtf.pdf
http://www.ptwoodturners.org/Tips%20and%
20Handouts/Methods%20and%20Jigs%20for%
20Reverse%20Turning%20Bowls.pdf

I love trying different woods, especially those
that don’t come up very often. So when my
neighbour cut down his mature rhododendron
ponticum (purple flowering variety) I jumped
at the chance to turn the 6” trunk. I was delighted with how well it turned and with the
great colour and grain. Chips were flying everywhere and I was having fun. Then I felt a
tiny itch on my neck. I brushed off some chips
and carried on but within a few minutes the
itch turned into a mild burning sensation and I
could feel welts rising on my neck. I stopped
turning and headed straight in for a shower
followed by calamine solution on the welts.
The next morning all was well but a little research yielded the following information from
Wikipedia.
…. suspect rhododendrons are Rhododendron ponticum (the purple variety,
ED) and Rhododendron luteum (a yellow variety I have never seen around
here ED), both originating in northern
Asia Minor.…. Rhododendron is extremely toxic to horses, with some animals dying within a few hours of ingesting the plant, although most horses tend to avoid it if they have access
to good forage.
I do not have reactions to many woods. Cocobolo makes me sneeze and cedar (red and
yellow) gives me a headache but otherwise I
have been pretty lucky. My reaction this time
may not be typical and I cannot speak for other
varieties of the plant. But fair warning is given
– rhododendrons just may fight back.
Bruce Campbell

Here are the four was of directly transferring photographs or graphics to wood that I demonstrated at the
meeting. There are other ways to transfer images but
they require an intermediary step. Most of these methods are for flat wood but you could use them to create
banding and then inlaying it into your turned piece. All
of these methods work with black and white or colour
images.
Choose wood that is a lighter colour with grain that will
compliment your photo. We will be using inkjet or laser
printers and they do NOT print white. So the wood
shows where the white would be. Make sure you have
raised the grain, finish sanded the wood and it is clean
and dry.
Inkjet and laser printers are not the same so please pay
special attention to which is being used in each method.
Inkjet printers also use two different kinds of ink. Dye
ink is the most common and it is not waterproof in
most cases, so you will not be able to add a finish. Pigment inks on the other hand are waterproof so finishes
can be applied. It is best to try it and see if your printer
works for you or not.
Method #1: Printing directly onto the wood using an
inkjet printer.
Make sure your printer can handle thick stock. Check
the manual to see what the thickest stock you can run
through it. The printer will usually have a way of putting the paper through it in a straight path, where the
paper does not bend at all. In my demo I used 1.5mm
plywood from Lee Valley Tools. They also carry an
0.8mm plywood which you could use for banding.
When you print onto wood make sure you use a matte
paper setting as the wood absorbs the ink, spreading
each ink dot a little, just like matte paper.
Remember to reverse (mirror) the image so your photo
comes out the correct way (specially if you have text)
and then just print on the wood as you would print on
paper and finish according to the type of ink your printer uses.
Method #2: Label Paper Transfer using your inkjet
printer.
This method uses the waxy paper found on the back of
address labels. Many people have used wax paper but I
found it not stiff enough for my printer. I remove all the
address labels from the backing and load it into the
printer so it will print on the glossy or waxy side. Reverse the image and print it as normal using the glossy
setting on your printer.
DO NOT TOUCH THE IMAGE. The ink does NOT dry
so anything you touch with the image will show. The
print will be slippery when you put it on the wood so
tape it down or hold it firmly in place. Roll or squeegee
the ink onto the wood making sure to cover the whole
area. Remove the waxy paper and apply a finish according to the ink you are using as described above.
Method #3: Gel Medium Transfer using a Laser Printer
of Photo Copy.
This method does NOT work with inkjet printers.
Reverse or mirror you image when printing it out on
your laser printer.
Brush an even layer of Gel Medium (I use Golden Soft
Gel (Gloss) # 3010-5, $20 at Opus). A reasonably thick
layer and make sure you cover the whole area your
print will be.
Lay the paper, print side to gel, onto the gelled area.
Tape it down or hold it firmly while you squeegee it
down. Make sure it is completely attached with no air
bubbles. Let it dry a couple of minutes or longer: Opus
said until the paper feels cold, others suggested overnight.
Rub the paper off using your finger or a cloth. I find
using a little water from a spray bottle makes it easier.
This is a time consuming step. Make sure all the paper
is removed.
Finishing is not necessary but I find it brings up the
colour. I use Golden Archival Gloss Mineral Spirit
Acrylic Varnish #5Q07731-X ($30 from Opus).
Method #4: Blender Pen Transfer using a Laser Printer
or Photo Copier
This method will NOT work with an inkjet print.
Print out your image in reverse (mirrored) on a laser

Colour it in with the blender pen. I use a Chartpak Pen

all these ingredients at your pharmacy.

Bruce Campbell
A Closer Look – the Collaborative Work of
Jay and Lin Mapson
Jay Mapson has been a
member of the Guild for
some time but recently his
wife, Lin, has been enhancing his work with pyrography. The effect is
quite charming, and just like tole painting on tinwork,
the burned images help to enhance the turned piece. I
wanted to speak with Jay and Lin to learn about their
collaboration and where they see it going.
Jay saw Lin’s artwork while they were getting to know
each other on-line so he sent her a set of coloured pencils. He really liked her work that seemed to, as he
says, “came spilling from the pencil.” Jay sees tremendous potential for her even though she has little formal
art training.
Lin, who was the head Public Relations for Chon Buri
Town Municipality in Thailand, knew nothing about
woodturning but really liked both the images and samples of Jay’s work that she saw. The collaboration of
her drawing and Jay’s turning took a while to develop
partly because of learning about pyrography and partly
because of hesitation to “practice” on Jay’s finished
pieces. She has gotten around that by purchasing thin
plywood and inexpensive birdhouses that she can practice on to refine her skills. She is also beginning to turn
wood by taking our Turning 101 classes and the Project
Days held by the Fraser Valley Guild. We are anxious
to see where that leads.
The Gold lid box
shown here was
purpose turned for
Lin to decorate but
she was a little unhappy with it. Jay
suggested they
paint the lid with
gold acrylic paint
and re-burn the pattern which gave better results. But the
nicer story is about
the box with the red
sides. The lid for the
box was the coffee
cup cover Jay had in
his shop. Lin found it and started burning a pattern
which turned out quite well. So Jay turned the bottom
from a piece of wood Lin got in a Turning 101 session.
While Jay has a number of forms that he has developed
over the years, Lin has yet to really find her own
“voice”. However, she is also a prolific photographer
and the images and scenery in Canada are having a
wonderful impact on her so perhaps that voice will
come soon.
Meanwhile, Jay says, “I have been thinking of shapes
that would go well with elephants and palm trees.”
We can expect to see more collaborative pieces from
them in the future and who knows where it will lead.
Lin wants to learn much more about her new home and
improve her language skills. And, of course, they are
creating a new life together.
So, thanks to the Jay and
Lin for the interesting collaborative work and congratulations on their first
wedding anniversary.
